modern:
The glorified weep no more, for *all outward causes of grief are gone*. There are no broken friendships and no ruined hopes in heaven. Poverty, famine, danger, persecution and slander are unknown there. No pain distresses, no thought of death or loss saddens. They weep no more, for *they are perfectly holy*. No “evil heart of unbelief” urges them to turn away from the living God. They are without fault before his throne, and fully shaped into his image. Well may those stop mourning who have stopped sinning. They weep no more, because *all fear of change is past*. They know they are eternally secure. Sin is shut out, and they are shut in. They live in a city that will never be stormed; they bask in a sun that will never set; they drink from a river that will never run dry; they pick fruit from a tree that will never wither. Countless ages may roll by, but eternity won’t be used up, and as long as eternity lasts, their immortality and happiness will last with it. They are forever with the Lord.

They weep no more, because *every desire is fulfilled*. They can’t wish for anything they don’t already have. Eye and ear, heart and hand, judgment, imagination, hope, desire, will—all their powers are completely satisfied. Imperfect as our present ideas are of the things God has prepared for those who love him, we know enough, by what the Spirit has revealed, to know that the saints above are supremely happy. The joy of Christ, an infinite fullness of delight, is in them. They bathe in the bottomless, shoreless sea of infinite blessedness. That same joyful rest remains for us, and it may not be far off. Before long the weeping willow will be exchanged for the palm branch of victory, and sorrow’s dewdrops will be turned into the pearls of everlasting joy. “Wherefore comfort one another with these words.”

modern: It is beyond measure desirable that we, as believers, should have the person of Jesus always before us, to set our love for him on fire and to increase our knowledge of him. I wish to God all my readers were enrolled as diligent students in Jesus’ college—students of Corpus Christi, the body of Christ—determined to earn a good degree in the learning of the cross. But to have Jesus always near, the heart must be full of him, welling up with his love, even to overflowing. That is why the apostle prays “that Christ may *dwell in your hearts*.” See how near he wants Jesus to be! You can’t get anything closer to you than having it in your very heart. “*That he may dwell*”: not that he may drop in on you now and then, as a casual visitor comes into a house and stays a night, but that he may *dwell*, that Jesus may become the Lord and Tenant of your inmost being, never to go out again.

Notice the words: that he may dwell *in your heart*, the best room in the house of our humanity; not in your thoughts alone, but in your love; not merely in the mind’s reflections, but in the heart’s feelings. We should long for a love for Christ of the most lasting kind: not a love that flares up and then dies down into the darkness of a few embers, but a constant flame, fed with sacred fuel, like the fire on the altar that never went out. This can’t be done except by faith. Faith must be strong, or love won’t be fervent; the root of the flower must be healthy, or we can’t expect the bloom to be sweet. Faith is the lily’s root, and love is the lily’s bloom. Now, reader, Jesus can’t be in your heart’s love unless you have a firm hold on him by your heart’s faith; so pray that you may always trust Christ, so that you may always love him. If love is cold, you can be sure faith is drooping.

modern:
Since Jesus has gone ahead of us, things aren’t as they would have been if he had never passed that way. He has *conquered every enemy* that blocked the road. Cheer up now, fainthearted soldier. Christ has not only traveled the road; he has killed your enemies. Are you afraid of sin? He has nailed it to his cross. Are you afraid of death? He has been the death of Death. Are you afraid of hell? He has barred it against the coming of any of his children; they will never see the pit of ruin. Whatever enemies may be in front of the Christian, they are all overcome. There are lions, but their teeth are broken; there are serpents, but their fangs are pulled out; there are rivers, but they are bridged or can be waded; there are flames, but we wear that matchless garment that makes us fireproof. The sword forged against us is already blunted; the weapons of war the enemy is preparing have already lost their point. In the person of Christ, God has taken away all the power anything can have to hurt us.

Well then, the army may safely march on, and you can go joyfully on your journey, for all your enemies are conquered beforehand. What will you do but march on to take the prey? They are beaten, they are defeated; all you have to do is divide the plunder. It’s true that you will often be in combat, but your fight will be with a defeated enemy. His head is crushed. He may try to hurt you, but his strength won’t be enough for his malicious plans. Your victory will be easy, and your treasure beyond all counting.

modern: But what restitution can someone make who scatters the firebrands of error or the coals of lust, and sets people’s souls ablaze with the fire of hell? The guilt is beyond reckoning, and the damage can’t be undone. If such an offender is forgiven, what grief it will cause him looking back, since he can’t undo the harm he has done! A bad example may light a flame that years of reformed character can’t put out. To burn people’s food is bad enough, but how much worse to destroy the soul! It may be useful to us to think about how far we may have been guilty in the past, and to ask whether, even now, there may be evil in us that tends to harm the souls of our relatives, friends or neighbors.

The fire of strife is a terrible evil when it breaks out in a Christian church. Where converts were multiplying and God was being glorified, jealousy and envy do the devil’s work most effectively. Where the golden grain was being brought in to reward the labor of the great Boaz, the fire of hostility comes in and leaves little but smoke and a heap of blackness. Woe to those through whom offenses come! May they never come through us; for although we can’t make restitution, we will certainly be the chief sufferers if we are the chief offenders. Those who feed the fire deserve fair blame, but whoever first lights it is most to blame. Discord usually catches hold first among the thorns. It is nursed among the hypocrites and base professors in the church, and off it goes among the righteous, blown by the winds of hell, and no one knows where it may end. O Lord and giver of peace, make us peacemakers, and never let us aid and abet the people of strife, or even unintentionally cause the least division among your people.

modern: In Scripture, faith is described under the picture of all the senses. It is *sight*: “Look unto me and be ye saved.” It is *hearing*: “Hear, and your soul shall live.” Faith is *smell*: “All thy garments smell of myrrh, and aloes, and cassia”; “thy name is as ointment poured forth.” Faith is spiritual *touch*. By this faith the woman came up behind and touched the hem of Christ’s garment, and by it we handle the things of the good word of life. Faith is equally the spirit’s taste. “How sweet are thy words to my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my lips.” “Except a man eat my flesh,” says Christ, *“and drink my blood, there is no life in him.”*

This “*taste*” is faith *in one of its highest activities*. One of the first things faith does is *hear*. We hear the voice of God, not with the outward ear alone but with the inward ear; we hear it as God’s Word, and we believe it to be so. That is the “hearing” of faith. Then our mind *looks* at the truth as it is set before us; that is, we understand it and grasp its meaning. That is the “seeing” of faith. Next we discover how precious it is; we begin to admire it and find how fragrant it is. That is faith in its “*smell*.” Then we take as our own the mercies prepared for us in Christ. That is faith in its “*touch*.” From this follow the enjoyments, the peace, the delight, the fellowship, which are faith in its “taste.” Any one of these acts of faith saves. To hear Christ’s voice as the sure voice of God in the soul will save us. But what gives true enjoyment is the side of faith in which Christ, by holy taste, is received into us and made, by an inward, spiritual sense of his sweetness and preciousness, the food of our souls. It is then that we sit “under his shadow with great delight,” and find his fruit sweet to our taste.

notes.note: “As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so is my beloved… I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit was sweet to my taste” ([[Song.2.3|Song of Solomon 2:3]]).

modern:
These words may answer your worries of conscience, devout reader, about *the ordinances*. Perhaps you say, “I’d be afraid to be baptized; it’s such a solemn thing to declare that I am dead with Christ and buried with him. I wouldn’t feel free to come to the Master’s table; I’d be afraid of eating and drinking damnation to myself, not discerning the Lord’s body.” Ah, poor trembler, Jesus has given you freedom; don’t be afraid. If a stranger came to your house, he would stand at the door or wait in the hall; he wouldn’t dream of barging uninvited into your living room—he isn’t at home there. But your child makes himself very free about the house, and so it is with the child of God. A stranger may not intrude where a child may go. When the Holy Spirit has made you feel the spirit of adoption, you can come to the Christian ordinances without fear.

The same rule holds for *the Christian’s inward privileges*. You think, poor seeker, that you aren’t allowed to rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory; if you are allowed inside Christ’s door, or to sit at the foot of his table, you will be well content. Ah, but you won’t have fewer privileges than the very greatest. God makes no difference in his love to his children. A child is a child to him. He won’t make him a hired servant; he will feast on the fatted calf and have the music and dancing as much as if he had never gone astray. When Jesus comes into the heart, he issues a general license to be glad in the Lord. No chains are worn in the court of King Jesus. Our entry into full privileges may be gradual, but it is sure. Perhaps our reader is saying, “I wish I could enjoy the promises, and walk at liberty in my Lord’s commands.” “If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest.” Loose the chains from your neck, O captive daughter, for Jesus sets you free.

modern:
The Lord’s people delight in the covenant itself. It is an unfailing source of comfort to them whenever the Holy Spirit leads them into its banqueting house and waves its banner of love. They love to think about *how old* that covenant is, remembering that before the morning star knew its place, or the planets ran their course, the interests of the saints were made secure in Christ Jesus. It is especially pleasing to them to remember *how sure* the covenant is, as they meditate on “the sure mercies of David.” They love to celebrate it as “signed, and sealed, and ratified, in all things ordered well.” It often makes their hearts swell with joy to think of its *unchangeableness*: a covenant that neither time nor eternity, life nor death, will ever be able to break; a covenant as old as eternity and as everlasting as the Rock of Ages.

They also rejoice to feast on *the fullness* of this covenant, for they see everything provided for them in it. God is their portion, Christ their companion, the Spirit their Comforter, earth their lodging, and heaven their home. They see in it an inheritance reserved and entailed to every soul who has a share in its ancient and eternal deed of gift. Their eyes sparkled when they found it as a treasure in the Bible; but oh, how their souls were gladdened when they saw in the last will and testament of their divine Kinsman that it was left to them! Above all, it is the pleasure of God’s people to think about *the graciousness* of this covenant. They see that the law was made void because it was a covenant of works and depended on merit; but they see that this one lasts, because grace is the basis, grace the condition, grace the theme, grace the rampart, grace the foundation, grace the topstone. The covenant is a treasury of wealth, a granary of food, a fountain of life, a storehouse of salvation, a charter of peace and a harbor of joy.

notes.term: He hath commanded his covenant for ever
Its banqueting house… its banner of love
notes.note: “He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love” ([[Song.2.4|Song of Solomon 2:4]]).

modern:
How great the difference between Moses and Jesus! When the prophet of Horeb had been forty days on the mountain, he went through a kind of transfiguration, so that his face shone with exceeding brightness, and he put a veil over it, for the people couldn’t bear to look at his glory. Not so our Savior. He had been transfigured with a greater glory than Moses had, and yet it isn’t written that the people were blinded by the blaze of his face. Rather, they were amazed, and they ran to him and greeted him. The glory of the law drives us away, but the greater glory of Jesus draws us. Though Jesus is holy and just, there is so much truth and grace blended with his purity that sinners run to him, amazed at his goodness and captivated by his love. They greet him, become his disciples and take him as their Lord and Master.

Reader, it may be that right now you are blinded by the dazzling brightness of the law of God. You feel its claims on your conscience, but you can’t keep it in your life. It isn’t that you find fault with the law; on the contrary, it commands your deepest respect. Still, it does nothing to draw you to God; if anything, you are hardened in heart and edging toward despair. Ah, poor heart! Turn your eye from Moses, with all his forbidding splendor, and look to Jesus, shining with gentler glories. See his flowing wounds and his thorn-crowned head! He is the Son of God, and in that he is greater than Moses; but he is the Lord of love, and in that he is more tender than the lawgiver. He bore the wrath of God, and in his death he revealed more of God’s justice than Sinai ablaze; but that justice has now been satisfied, and from now on it is the guardian of those who believe in Jesus. Look, sinner, to the bleeding Savior, and as you feel the pull of his love, fly to his arms, and you will be saved.

modern:
*Work with all diligence to keep out that monster unbelief*. It dishonors Christ so much that he will withdraw his felt presence if we insult him by indulging it. It is true that it is a weed whose seeds we can never completely root out of the soil, but we must strike at its root with zeal and persistence. Of all hateful things it is the most to be loathed. Its harm is so poisonous that both the one who shows it and the one it is shown to are hurt by it. In your case, believer, it is most wicked, for your Lord’s mercies in the past increase your guilt in doubting him now. When you distrust the Lord Jesus, he may well cry out, “Behold I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves.” This is crowning his head with thorns of the sharpest kind. It is very cruel for a dearly loved wife to mistrust a kind and faithful husband. The sin is needless, foolish and unjustified. Jesus has never given the slightest ground for suspicion, and it is hard to be doubted by those to whom our conduct has always been loving and true.

Jesus is the Son of the Highest, and has boundless wealth; it is shameful to doubt Omnipotence and distrust all-sufficiency. The cattle on a thousand hills will be enough for our hungriest feeding, and the granaries of heaven aren’t likely to be emptied by our eating. If Christ were only a cistern, we might soon drain his fullness; but who can drain a fountain? Countless spirits have drawn their supplies from him, and not one of them has complained of any shortage in his resources. Away, then, with this lying traitor unbelief, for his only errand is to cut the bonds of fellowship and make us mourn an absent Savior. Bunyan tells us that unbelief has “as many lives as a cat”; if so, let’s kill one life now, and keep at the work until all nine are gone. Down with you, traitor; my heart loathes you.

modern: These words have often been used by holy men in the hour of their death. We can profitably think about them this evening. What the faithful man cares about most, in life and in death, isn’t his body or his property but his spirit. This is his choice treasure; if it is safe, all is well. What is this mortal condition compared with the soul? The believer commits his soul into the hand of his God. It came from him; it is his own; he has kept it until now; he is able to keep it; and it is most fitting that he should receive it. All things are safe in Jehovah’s hands. Whatever we entrust to the Lord will be secure, both now and in that day of days we are hurrying toward. It is peaceful living and glorious dying to rest in the care of heaven. We should commit our all into Jesus’ faithful hand at all times. Then, though life may hang by a thread and troubles may multiply like the sands of the sea, our soul will live at ease and delight in quiet resting places.

“*Thou hast redeemed me, O Lord God of truth*.” Redemption is a solid basis for confidence. David hadn’t known Calvary as we have, but earthly deliverance cheered him; and won’t eternal redemption comfort us more sweetly still? Past deliverances are strong arguments for present help. What the Lord has done, he will do again, for he doesn’t change. He is faithful to his promises and gracious to his saints; he won’t turn away from his people.

notes.note: David’s prayer in [[Ps.31.5|Psalm 31:5]], used by Jesus as he died: “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” ([[Luke.23.46|Luke 23:46]]); compare Stephen in [[Acts.7.59|Acts 7:59]].

modern: My soul, how much you need this, for your lamp won’t keep burning long without it. Your wick will smoke and become offensive if the light goes out, and go out it will if there is no oil. You have no well of oil springing up in your human nature, so you must go to those who sell and buy for yourself, or like the foolish virgins you will have to cry, “My lamp is gone out.” Even the consecrated lamps couldn’t give light without oil. Though they shone in the tabernacle, they needed to be fed; though no rough winds blew on them, they needed to be trimmed; and your need is just as great. Even in the happiest circumstances you can’t give light for another hour unless fresh oil of grace is given to you.

Not just any oil could be used in the Lord’s service. Neither the petroleum that oozes so plentifully out of the earth, nor oil from fish, nor oil pressed from nuts would be accepted. Only one oil was chosen, and that the best olive oil. Pretended grace from natural goodness, imagined grace from priestly hands or fancied grace from outward ceremonies will never do for the true saint of God. He knows the Lord wouldn’t be pleased with rivers of such oil. He goes to the olive press of Gethsemane and draws his supplies from him who was crushed there. The oil of gospel grace is pure and free from sediment and dregs, and so the light it feeds is clear and bright. Our churches are the Savior’s golden lampstands, and if they are to be lights in this dark world, they must have plenty of holy oil. Let’s pray for ourselves, our ministers and our churches, that they may never lack oil for the light. Truth, holiness, joy, knowledge, love: these are all beams of the sacred light, but we can’t give them out unless we receive oil in private from God the Holy Spirit.

modern: Though we have borne some fruit for Christ, and have a joyful hope that we are “plants of his own right hand planting,” there are times when we feel very barren. Prayer is lifeless, love is cold, faith is weak; every grace in the garden of our heart wilts and droops. We are like flowers in the hot sun, needing a refreshing shower. In such a condition, what are we to do? The text is spoken to us in exactly that state. “*Sing, O barren, break forth and cry aloud*.” But what can I sing about? I can’t talk about the present, and even the past looks full of barrenness. Ah, I can sing of Jesus Christ. I can talk about the visits the Redeemer has paid me before; or if not of these, I can magnify the great love with which he loved his people when he came from the heights of heaven to redeem them. I will go to the cross again. Come, my soul, you were heavily burdened once, and you lost your burden there. Go to Calvary again. Perhaps the very cross that gave you life will give you fruitfulness. What is my barrenness? It is the platform for his fruit-creating power. What is my desolation? It is the black setting for the sapphire of his everlasting love. I will go in poverty, I will go in helplessness, I will go in all my shame and backsliding; I will tell him that I am still his child, and in confidence in his faithful heart, even I, the barren one, will sing and cry aloud.

Sing, believer, for it will cheer your own heart and the hearts of other desolate ones. Sing on, for now that you are really ashamed of being barren, you will soon be fruitful. Now that God makes you *unwilling* to be without fruit, he will soon cover you with clusters. The experience of our barrenness is painful, but the Lord’s visits are delightful. A sense of our own poverty drives us to Christ, and that is where we need to be, for in him our fruit is found.

modern: When Dr. Carey was suffering from a dangerous illness, someone asked him, “If this sickness should prove fatal, what passage would you select as the text for your funeral sermon?” He replied, “Oh, I feel that such a poor sinful creature is unworthy to have anything said about him; but if a funeral sermon must be preached, let it be from the words, ‘Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness; according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.’” In the same spirit of humility, he directed in his will that the following inscription, and nothing more, should be cut on his gravestone:

Only on the ground of free grace can the most experienced and most honored of the saints come to their God. The best of men are aware, more than anyone, that they are only men at their best. Empty boats float high, but heavily loaded ships sit low in the water. Mere professors can boast, but true children of God cry for mercy on their unprofitableness. We need the Lord to have mercy on our good works, our prayers, our preaching, our giving to the poor and our holiest things. The blood wasn’t only sprinkled on the doorposts of Israel’s houses, but on the sanctuary, the mercy-seat and the altar, because sin creeps into our holiest things, and the blood of Jesus is needed to cleanse them from defilement. If mercy must be shown toward our duties, what are we to say about our sins? How sweet to remember that inexhaustible mercy is waiting to be gracious to us, to heal our backslidings and make our broken bones rejoice!

Nazirites had taken, among other vows, one that barred them from drinking wine. So that they wouldn’t break the promise, they were forbidden to drink wine vinegar or strong drink; and to make the rule still clearer, they weren’t to touch the unfermented juice of grapes, or even eat the fruit, fresh or dried. Altogether, to keep the vow intact, they weren’t allowed anything to do with the vine at all; in fact, they were to avoid the appearance of evil. Surely this is a lesson to the Lord’s separated ones, teaching them to come away from sin in every form; to avoid not only its grosser shapes, but even its spirit and its likeness.

Strict living is much despised these days, but rest assured, dear reader, it is both the safest and the happiest. Whoever gives way to the world on a point or two is in fearful danger; whoever eats the grapes of Sodom will soon drink the wine of Gomorrah. A little crack in a sea wall in Holland lets the sea in, and the gap quickly widens until a whole province is drowned. Fitting in with the world, to any degree, is a snare to the soul, and makes it more and more prone to presumptuous sins. Moreover, just as the Nazirite who drank grape juice couldn’t be quite sure it hadn’t fermented a little, and so couldn’t be clear in his heart that his vow was unbroken, so the yielding, compromising Christian can’t have a conscience free of offense, but must feel that the monitor within has doubts about him. We needn’t be in any doubt about doubtful things: they are wrong for us. We mustn’t toy with tempting things, but run from them quickly. Better to be sneered at as a Puritan than despised as a hypocrite. Careful living may involve a great deal of self-denial, but it has pleasures of its own that more than make up for it.

modern:
It may seem an easy thing to wait, but it is one of the postures a Christian soldier learns only after years of training. Marching, and quick marching, come far more easily to God’s warriors than standing still. There are hours of bewilderment when the most willing spirit, eager to serve the Lord, doesn’t know which way to turn. What should it do then? Torment itself with despair? Run back in cowardice, turn aside in fear, or rush forward in presumption? No, it should simply wait.

*Wait in prayer*, though. Call on God and lay the case out before him. Tell him your difficulty, and plead his promise of help. When torn between one duty and another, it is sweet to be as humble as a child and *wait with simplicity of soul* on the Lord. It is sure to go well with us when we feel and know our own foolishness and are wholeheartedly willing to be guided by the will of God. But *wait in faith*. Show your unshaken confidence in him; for unfaithful, untrusting waiting is just an insult to the Lord. Believe that even if he keeps you waiting until midnight, he will still come at the right time; the vision will come and won’t be late. *Wait in quiet patience*, not rebelling because you are under the affliction, but blessing your God for it. Never grumble against the second cause, as the children of Israel did against Moses. Never wish you could go back to the world again, but accept the case as it is, and put it as it stands, simply and wholeheartedly, without any self-will, into the hand of your covenant God, saying, “Now, Lord, not my will, but yours be done. I don’t know what to do; I am brought to the end of my resources; but I will wait until you split the floods or drive back my enemies. I will wait, if you keep me many a day, for my heart is fixed on you alone, O God, and my spirit waits for you in the full conviction that you will yet be my joy and my salvation, my refuge and my strong tower.”

modern:
*“I have seen his ways, and will heal him.”*

[[Isa.57.18|Isaiah 57:18]]

It is God’s right alone to remove spiritual disease. Natural disease may be healed through human means, but even then the honor is to be given to God, who gives medicine its power and gives the human body the strength to throw off disease. As for spiritual sicknesses, these belong to the great Physician alone. He claims it as his own right: “I kill and I make alive, I wound and I heal”; and one of the Lord’s choice titles is Jehovah-Rophi, “the Lord that healeth thee.” “I will heal thee of thy wounds” is a promise that couldn’t come from the lips of man, only from the mouth of the eternal God. That is why the psalmist cried to the Lord, “O Lord, heal me, for my bones are sore vexed,” and again, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against thee.” And that is why the godly praise the name of the Lord, saying, “He healeth all our diseases.” He who made man can restore man; he who first created our nature can create it anew. What a surpassing comfort it is that in the person of Jesus “dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily!”

My soul, whatever your disease may be, this great Physician can heal you. If he is God, there can be no limit to his power. Come, then, with the blind eye of a darkened understanding; come with the limping foot of wasted energy; come with the crippled hand of weak faith, the fever of an angry temper or the shivering fits of despondency. Come just as you are, for he who is God can certainly heal you of your plague. No one will hold back the healing power that comes out of Jesus our Lord. Legions of devils have been made to acknowledge the power of the beloved Physician, and he has never once been baffled. All his patients have been cured in the past and will be in the future, and you will be one of them, my friend, if only you will rest yourself on him tonight.

modern:
In times of severe trial, the Christian has nothing on earth he can trust, and so he is forced to throw himself on his God alone. When his ship is on her side and no human rescue can help, he must simply and entirely trust himself to the providence and care of God. Happy storm, that wrecks a man on such a rock as this! Oh, blessed hurricane, that drives the soul to God and God alone! Sometimes we can’t get at our God because of the crowd of our friends; but when a man is so poor, so friendless, so helpless that he has nowhere else to turn, he flies into his Father’s arms and is blessedly held there! When he is weighed down with troubles so pressing and so private that he can’t tell them to anyone but his God, he may be thankful for them, for he will learn more of his Lord then than at any other time.

Oh, storm-tossed believer, it is a happy trouble that drives you to your Father! Now that you have only your God to trust, make sure you put your full confidence in him. Don’t dishonor your Lord and Master with unworthy doubts and fears, but be strong in faith, giving glory to God. Show the world that your God is worth ten thousand worlds to you. Show rich men how rich you are in your poverty when the Lord God is your helper. Show the strong man how strong you are in your weakness when underneath you are the everlasting arms. Now is the time for feats of faith and brave exploits. Be strong and very courageous, and the Lord your God will certainly, as surely as he built the heavens and the earth, glorify himself in your weakness and show his might in the middle of your distress. The grandeur of the arch of heaven would be spoiled if the sky were held up by a single visible column, and your faith would lose its glory if it rested on anything the eye of flesh can see. May the Holy Spirit help you rest in Jesus on this last day of the month.

modern:
As he is in the light! Can we ever reach that? Will we ever be able to walk as clearly in the light as he whom we call “Our Father,” of whom it is written, “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all”? Certainly this is the model set before us, for the Savior himself said, “Be ye perfect, even as your Father who is in heaven is perfect”; and although we may feel that we can never rival God’s perfection, we are still to pursue it and never be satisfied until we reach it. The young artist taking up his first brush can hardly hope to equal Raphael or Michelangelo; but still, if he didn’t have a noble ideal of perfection before his mind, he would only reach something very poor and ordinary.

But what does it mean that the Christian is to walk in the light as God is in the light? We take it to mean *likeness*, not *degree*. We are as truly in the light, as wholeheartedly in the light, as sincerely in the light, as honestly in the light, though we can’t be there in the same measure. I can’t live in the sun; it is too bright a place for me to live in; but I can *walk* in the light of the sun. In the same way, though I can’t reach the perfection of purity and truth that belongs by nature to the Lord of hosts as the infinitely good, I can set the Lord always before me and strive, with the help of the Spirit within me, to be shaped into his image. That famous old commentator John Trapp says, “We may be in the light as God is in the light for *quality*, but not for *equality*.” We are to have the same light, and are to have it and walk in it as truly as God does; but equality with God in his holiness and purity must wait until we cross the Jordan and enter the perfection of the Most High. Notice that the blessings of holy fellowship and perfect cleansing are bound up with walking in the light.
